newsitem.title: UK: Emerging market debt up on Dow, Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market debt up on Dow, Treasuries.

text.p: Emerging market debt prices were higher on Tuesday as a sharp rise in U.S. stock prices on Monday and a stable U.S. Treasury market lured buyers back into the market, traders said.

"What seemed like a strong close in the Dow and reasonably stable Treasuries put more confidence into the market and people started to take more paper on board," said a Brady bond trader at a European investment bank.
Bulgarian debt, which widened by about 25 to 30 basis points on Monday, scored the biggest gains today with its IABS rising 3/4 to 78-1/4 bid and its FLRBs firming 7/8 to63 bid.

"We saw some tightening this morning on the back of yesterday's rally in the Dow. Bulgaria gave up 30 basis points but it has clawed back most of its losses," said a Brady trader at a major U.S. investment bank in London.
Russian dollar-denominated Vnesheconombank loans also recouped some recent losses, rising one full percentage point to 101-3/4 bid.

However, traders said volumes were expected to remain light ahead of today's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) though the market does not expect the policy setting committee to raise U.S. interest rates.
"We do have the FOMC which one must not forget about. Nobody is expecting anything but nonetheless you need to keep an eye on what's going on," a trader at a U.S. investment bank said.
Market strategists also said the Brady market was likely keep a close eye on the Hong Kong dollar and the Heng Seng index.

"I think that is almost more important than U.S. Treasuries because if the Hong Kong dollar really comes under pressure it is more because of global liquidity concerns rather than fundamentals so that will have an impact on our market," said Ingrid Iverson, debt straytegist at UBS Securities.
Even still, strategists said investors were likely to continue to buy emerging market paper on weakness because the fundamentals for many countries remained favourable.

"There is still money in the market and when spreads widen out people start to see value and obviously there is no fundamental reason for selling any of these countries so its not surprising that they bounced back," said Iverson.
